processing: Light oxidation and semi-ball rolling with little or no roast, as with other Taiwanese high-mountain oolong.
harvest_season: The lots on record are spring pickings, harvested in May; winter lots are typical of the class.
appearance_liquor: Pale clear yellow-green when unroasted, typical of high-mountain oolong.
appearance_wet: Thick, supple whole leaves that open completely, typical of high-altitude tea.
taste_profile: As with other high-altitude Taiwanese oolongs, expect floral sweetness, a dense soft body and little bitterness, with a cooling finish in good lots.

brewing.notes: Good leaf will take many steeps. Use a long first steep and do not rush it with cool water.

vintage_note: Sold by year and season, spring being the usual listing. Unroasted lots are best within a year or so of picking, kept sealed and cool.
description:
Qi Lai Shan oolong is a high-mountain tea from the slopes around Qilai Mountain in the Ren'ai area of Nantou, and Qilaishan is among the mountain names most often attached to Taiwan's high-mountain oolongs. One seller says gardens here are typically at or above about 1,500 metres, and one tasting note records a 2,200-metre lot, so treat any single figure with care.

It is usually Qing Xin Oolong made in the light, rolled style.

The general high-mountain pattern applies: floral sweetness over a thick texture and low bitterness. Near-boiling water and a patient first steep will show you more than delicate treatment will.

Buy from a seller who names the harvest and, ideally, the garden. The mountain name is widely used, and the leaf itself is the real check, with thick whole leaves after brewing being a good sign.
history: Little is documented about when the gardens were planted. Commercial tea in Ren'ai grew from planting promoted around Wushe and Gaofeng, and Qilaishan has since become one of the recognised names for Taiwanese high-mountain oolong.
